Many interesting wave phenomena -- like fluid dynamics, lasers, and water
waves -- are described by nonlinear hyperbolic partial differential equations.
The solutions of these problems often contain discontinuities.  So-called
**limiters** (sometimes referred to as *slope limiters* or *flux limiters*)
are one of the key ingredients in approximating these discontinuous solutions.
This page explains how to interpolate non-smooth data without creating
wiggles.

It is an HTML version of a
[Jupyter notebook](https://github.com/ketch/HyperPython/blob/master/Guide_to_limiters.ipynb)
from my [HyperPython](https://github.com/ketch/HyperPython) course.  The
notebook includes a Python implementation of everything shown here, which you
can run and modify; some of that code is reproduced below in collapsible
boxes.  On this page, the computations run in your browser, except for the
advection solutions at the end, which were computed with
[PyClaw](https://www.clawpack.org/pyclaw/).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Shared functions for the piecewise-linear interpolants.
lib = {
  const x = d3.range(-4, 5);  // sample points -4, -3, ..., 4
  const datasets = {
    "Smooth": x.map(t => Math.sin(t / 2) + 1),
    "Discontinuous": x.map(t => Math.sin(t / 2) + 1 + 2 * (t > 0)),
    "Monotone": x.map(t => Math.exp(t / 3))
  };

  function phi(theta, limiter) {
    switch (limiter) {
      case "minmod": return Math.max(0, Math.min(1, theta));
      case "van Leer": return (theta + Math.abs(theta)) / (1 + Math.abs(theta));
      case "MC": return Math.max(0, Math.min((1 + theta) / 2, 2, 2 * theta));
      case "superbee": return Math.max(0, Math.min(1, 2 * theta), Math.min(2, theta));
      default: throw new Error("Unrecognized limiter: " + limiter);
    }
  }
  const limiters = ["minmod", "van Leer", "superbee", "MC"];
  const differences = ["centered", "forward", "backward"];

  // Slope sigma_i at each sample point.  Points where the needed data is
  // missing (the ends), and limited slopes with B_i = 0, get sigma_i = 0.
  function slopes(y, method) {
    const n = y.length, s = new Array(n).fill(0);
    const F = i => (y[i + 1] - y[i]) / (x[i + 1] - x[i]);
    const B = i => (y[i] - y[i - 1]) / (x[i] - x[i - 1]);
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      if (method === "piecewise constant") s[i] = 0;
      else if (method === "centered") s[i] = (i > 0 && i < n - 1) ? (y[i + 1] - y[i - 1]) / (x[i + 1] - x[i - 1]) : 0;
      else if (method === "forward") s[i] = i < n - 1 ? F(i) : 0;
      else if (method === "backward") s[i] = i > 0 ? B(i) : 0;
      else if (limiters.includes(method)) {
        if (i > 0 && i < n - 1 && B(i) !== 0) s[i] = phi(F(i) / B(i), method) * B(i);
      } else throw new Error("Unrecognized method: " + method);
    }
    return s;
  }

  // End points of each linear piece.  The piece around x_i extends to the
  // midpoints between x_i and its neighbors (and stops at the first and last
  // sample points).  Consecutive pieces are joined by vertical jumps.
  function pieces(y, s) {
    const n = y.length, pts = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      const a = i === 0 ? x[0] : (x[i - 1] + x[i]) / 2;
      const b = i === n - 1 ? x[n - 1] : (x[i] + x[i + 1]) / 2;
      pts.push({x: a, y: y[i] + s[i] * (a - x[i])}, {x: b, y: y[i] + s[i] * (b - x[i])});
    }
    return pts;
  }

  // Total variation: of the data, and of the piecewise-linear function
  // (changes along the pieces plus the sizes of the jumps).
  const tvData = y => d3.sum(y.slice(1), (v, i) => Math.abs(v - y[i]));
  const tvPieces = pts => d3.sum(pts.slice(1), (p, i) => Math.abs(p.y - pts[i].y));

  // Plot of the data and one piecewise-linear interpolant.
  function plot(y, s, {label = null, yDomain = [-0.5, 4.8], height = 210, boxes = false} = {}) {
    const pts = pieces(y, s);
    const boxData = boxes ? d3.range(1, y.length - 1).map(i => ({
      x1: (x[i - 1] + x[i]) / 2, x2: (x[i] + x[i + 1]) / 2,
      y1: (y[i - 1] + y[i]) / 2, y2: (y[i] + y[i + 1]) / 2
    })) : [];
    return Plot.plot({
      width: 700, height,
      marginTop: 10,
      x: {domain: [-4, 4], label: null},
      y: {domain: yDomain, label: null, grid: true},
      marks: [
        Plot.rect(boxData, {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: "y1", y2: "y2", fill: "gray", fillOpacity: 0.35}),
        Plot.line(pts, {x: "x", y: "y", strokeWidth: 2, clip: true}),
        Plot.dot(x.map((t, i) => ({x: t, y: y[i]})), {x: "x", y: "y", r: 6, fill: "red", fillOpacity: 0.5}),
        label ? Plot.text([label], {text: d => d, frameAnchor: "bottom-right", dx: -8, dy: -8, fontSize: 14}) : null
      ]
    });
  }

  return {x, datasets, phi, limiters, differences, slopes, pieces, tvData, tvPieces, plot};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Table of TV and range for several methods applied to one data set.
function tvTable(y, methods) {
  const fmt = v => v.toFixed(3);
  const rows = methods.map(m => {
    const pts = lib.pieces(y, lib.slopes(y, m));
    return html`<tr><td>${m}</td><td>${fmt(lib.tvPieces(pts))}</td>
            <td>${fmt(d3.min(pts, p => p.y))}</td><td>${fmt(d3.max(pts, p => p.y))}</td></tr>`;
  });
  return html`<table class="table table-sm" style="max-width: 32rem">
    <thead><tr><th>Slopes</th><th>Total variation</th><th>Minimum</th><th>Maximum</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td><em>data</em></td><td>${fmt(lib.tvData(y))}</td><td>${fmt(d3.min(y))}</td><td>${fmt(d3.max(y))}</td></tr>
      ${rows}
    </tbody></table>`;
}
```

## Interpolation and wiggles

Suppose you're given a set of data samples:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 210, marginTop: 10,
  x: {domain: [-5, 5], label: null},
  y: {domain: [-0.1, 2.1], label: null, grid: true},
  marks: [Plot.dot(lib.x.map((t, i) => ({x: t, y: lib.datasets.Smooth[i]})),
                   {x: "x", y: "y", r: 6, fill: "red", fillOpacity: 0.5})]
})
```

Now what you really want to know is, what is the state of the system at the
points halfway between your samples?  And to figure that out, you need to
guess at what's going on at the points in between those samples.  The
simplest approximation would be to assume that the system just jumps from one
value to the next somewhere in between:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
lib.plot(lib.datasets.Smooth, lib.slopes(lib.datasets.Smooth, "piecewise constant"),
         {label: "Piecewise-constant approximation", yDomain: [-0.1, 2.1]})
```

For this set of data, you don't really believe that's what's happening, do
you?  But our goal is to deal with systems that exhibit non-smooth (possibly
discontinuous) behavior, so we need to at least admit the possibility of
sudden jumps.  That's why we won't simply "connect the dots" to get a
continuous approximation.

Instead, we can try to approximate the slope around each of our sample points.
The simplest way to do so is using finite differences.  If we let $\sigma_i$
denote our approximation of the slope at $x_i$, then three common
approximations are:

- Forward difference: $\sigma_i = \dfrac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{x_{i+1}-x_i}$
- Backward difference: $\sigma_i = \dfrac{y_i - y_{i-1}}{x_i - x_{i-1}}$
- Centered difference: $\sigma_i = \dfrac{y_{i+1}-y_{i-1}}{x_{i+1}-x_{i-1}}$

Here's what each of these approximations looks like for our data:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`${lib.differences.map(m => lib.plot(lib.datasets.Smooth, lib.slopes(lib.datasets.Smooth, m),
                                         {label: m, yDomain: [-0.1, 2.1], height: 170}))}`
```

I've used $\sigma=0$ for the points at the edges where we don't have enough
data to compute the appropriate slope.

## The problem: overshoots!

Looking closely, you can see that each of these approximations adds little
jumps (called "overshoots") in some region where the data itself was
monotone.  Worse still, each of them generates negative values, whereas the
original values were non-negative!  If our data represent concentrations or
probabilities, then we have no way to make sense of negative values.  The
table below shows the minimum value of each approximation, and its total
variation, which we'll define [below](#total-variation).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tvTable(lib.datasets.Smooth, lib.differences)
```

Things look even worse if we take data samples from a function that is in
fact discontinuous:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`${lib.differences.map(m => lib.plot(lib.datasets.Discontinuous, lib.slopes(lib.datasets.Discontinuous, m),
                                         {label: m, height: 170}))}`
```

Now all three approaches have large, obvious overshoots.  This becomes even
more problematic when actually solving a hyperbolic PDE; see
[Lesson 3 of my HyperPython course](https://nbviewer.org/github/ketch/HyperPython/blob/master/Lesson_03_High-resolution_methods.ipynb)
for details.

Is there a better way?

## The simplest limiter: minmod

We'd like to avoid those overshoots and ensure that monotone regions of the
data give monotone interpolations.  For equally spaced points, we can do that
by choosing the slope $\sigma_i$ small enough that the interpolant near $x_i$
stays bounded between the neighboring averages $(y_{i-1}+y_i)/2$ and
$(y_i+y_{i+1})/2$.  There's an easy way to do that: just compute the forward
and backward differences (like we did above), and then use *whichever is
smaller* in absolute value.  If $y_i$ is an extremum, then to avoid increasing
the overall range of the data we always choose $\sigma_i=0$.

Here's what that looks like:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
lib.plot(lib.datasets.Discontinuous, lib.slopes(lib.datasets.Discontinuous, "minmod"),
         {label: "Minmod approximation"})
```

Let's apply minmod to a monotone sequence of values, to illustrate the
average-boundedness property:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
lib.plot(lib.datasets.Monotone, lib.slopes(lib.datasets.Monotone, "minmod"),
         {label: "Minmod approximation", yDomain: [-0.1, 4.1], height: 300, boxes: true})
```

Each grey box extends from the average of $y_i$ and its left neighbor,
$(y_{i-1}+y_i)/2$, to the average of $y_i$ and its right neighbor,
$(y_i+y_{i+1})/2$.  The minmod interpolant around $x_i$ is guaranteed to stay
within these bounds, so the right edge of one interpolated piece never
"overshoots" the left edge of the next.

## Total variation

In fact, the minmod limiter guarantees an important mathematical property: the
piecewise-linear function it produces has no more total variation (TV) than
the data.  For discrete data, TV is defined as

$$ TV(y) = \sum_i |y_i - y_{i-1}|.$$

For a piecewise-linear function with jumps, the TV is the sum of the absolute
changes along each linear piece plus the absolute size of each jump.
Essentially, TV is a measure of how much a function wiggles!  This *total
variation diminishing* (TVD) property is important because the true solutions
of scalar hyperbolic PDEs have the same property: their total variation never
increases.

In the 1970s and 80s, researchers developed many other limiters.  Most of them
do *not* guarantee that the interpolant has no more TV than the data.
Instead, they guarantee that the full numerical method for a scalar hyperbolic
PDE is TVD, as long as the time step is small enough.  These are known as
*TVD limiters*.

## TVD limiters

Just for fun, let's look at 3 more such limiters.  Let $F_i$ and $B_i$ denote
the forward- and backward-difference slope approximations at point $i$, and
let $\theta_i = F_i/B_i$ be their ratio.  Each of these limiters can be
described in terms of a function $\phi(\theta)$; the slope to be used is

$$\sigma_i = \phi(\theta_i) B_i.$$

(If $B_i = 0$, we take $\sigma_i = 0$.)  For instance, minmod corresponds to
$\phi(\theta) = \max(0,\min(1,\theta))$.  The other limiter names and
functions are:

- Monotonized centered difference (**MC**): $\phi(\theta) = \max\left(0,\min\left(\frac{1+\theta}{2},2,2\theta\right)\right)$
- **van Leer**: $\phi(\theta) = \dfrac{\theta + |\theta|}{1+ |\theta|}$
- **Superbee**: $\phi(\theta) = \max(0,\min(1,2\theta),\min(2,\theta))$

<details>
<summary>Python code from the notebook</summary>

```python
def phi(theta,limiter):
    if limiter == 'minmod':
        phi = np.maximum(0,np.minimum(1,theta))
    elif limiter == 'vanleer':
        phi = (theta + np.abs(theta))/(1+np.abs(theta))
    elif limiter == 'MC':
        phi = np.maximum(0,np.minimum( (1.+theta)/2., np.minimum(2.,2*theta)))
    elif limiter == 'superbee':
        phi = np.maximum(0,np.maximum(np.minimum(1.,2*theta),np.minimum(2.,theta)))
    else:
        raise ValueError('Unrecognized limiter: '+limiter)
    return phi

def limited_slopes(x,y,limiter='minmod'):
    "Slopes sigma_i = phi(theta_i) B_i, with sigma = 0 at the endpoints and wherever B_i = 0."
    forward  = np.zeros_like(y)
    backward = np.zeros_like(y)
    theta    = np.zeros_like(y)

    forward[:-1] = (y[1:]-y[:-1])/(x[1:]-x[:-1])
    backward[1:] = (y[1:]-y[:-1])/(x[1:]-x[:-1])
    interior = np.zeros(len(y),dtype=bool); interior[1:-1] = True
    nonzero = interior & (backward != 0)
    theta[nonzero] = forward[nonzero]/backward[nonzero]

    sigma = phi(theta,limiter) * backward
    sigma[~nonzero] = 0.
    return sigma
```

</details>

Here's what each of them looks like for our data.  You can also switch to the
smooth data we started with.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof tvdData = Inputs.radio(["Discontinuous", "Smooth"], {value: "Discontinuous", label: "Data"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const y = lib.datasets[tvdData];
  const yDomain = tvdData === "Smooth" ? [-0.1, 2.1] : [-0.1, 4.4];
  return html`${lib.limiters.map(m => {
    const s = lib.slopes(y, m);
    return lib.plot(y, s, {label: `${m} (TV = ${lib.tvPieces(lib.pieces(y, s)).toFixed(3)})`,
                           yDomain, height: 170});
  })}`;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tvTable(lib.datasets[tvdData], lib.limiters)
```

Compare these with [the finite difference approximations above](#the-problem-overshoots).

You'll notice that -- except for minmod -- all the limiters *do* produce some
overshoot near the discontinuity; the total variation of each of their
interpolants is larger than that of the data.  Superbee even increases the
total variation for the smooth data we used at the start.

What gives?  Well, these limiters are used within a larger algorithm for
solving hyperbolic PDEs.  It turns out that if the overshoots are small
enough, they are removed in a full step of the algorithm: for the advection
equation, the methods based on these limiters are TVD as long as the CFL
number is at most 1, even though the interpolants themselves are not.  So no
oscillations appear in the PDE solution.

### Interactive comparison

In each region, these limiters take three data points and give back a linear
interpolant.  It's illuminating to compare their behavior on a single set of
3 points: $(-1, y_{i-1})$, $(0, 0)$, and $(1, y_{i+1})$.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof y1 = Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: -0.3, step: 0.1, label: tex`y_{i-1}`})
viewof y3 = Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: 0.8, step: 0.1, label: tex`y_{i+1}`})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
threePoint = {
  const F = y3, B = -y1;   // forward and backward differences at x = 0
  const sigma = Object.fromEntries(lib.limiters.map(m =>
    [m, B === 0 ? 0 : lib.phi(F / B, m) * B]));
  return {F, B, sigma};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const xx = d3.range(-0.5, 0.5001, 0.01);
  const lines = lib.limiters.flatMap(m => xx.map(t => ({x: t, y: threePoint.sigma[m] * t, limiter: m})));
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 700, height: 360,
    x: {domain: [-1.1, 1.1], label: null},
    y: {domain: [-1.1, 1.1], label: null, grid: true},
    color: {legend: true, domain: lib.limiters},
    marks: [
      Plot.areaY(xx, {x: d => d, y1: d => threePoint.F * d, y2: d => threePoint.B * d,
                      fill: "gray", fillOpacity: 0.4}),
      Plot.line(lines, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "limiter", z: "limiter", strokeWidth: 2.5, strokeOpacity: 0.8}),
      Plot.dot([[-1, y1], [0, 0], [1, y3]], {x: d => d[0], y: d => d[1], r: 8, fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.5})
    ]
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<table class="table table-sm" style="max-width: 32rem">
  <thead><tr><th></th><th>Slope</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td><em>backward difference</em> ${tex`B`}</td><td>${threePoint.B.toFixed(3)}</td></tr>
    <tr><td><em>forward difference</em> ${tex`F`}</td><td>${threePoint.F.toFixed(3)}</td></tr>
    ${lib.limiters.map(m => html`<tr><td>${m}</td><td>${threePoint.sigma[m].toFixed(3)}</td></tr>`)}
  </tbody></table>`
```

The shaded region in the plot above shows the slopes that lie between the
backward difference and the forward difference.  For smooth data, both of
these differences approximate the derivative to first order, so any slope in
this region gives an interpolant that is second-order accurate.  All four
limiters always choose a slope in this region.  Play with the sliders and
answer the following questions:

- Which limiter usually chooses the flattest approximation?  Does it always?
- Which limiter usually chooses the steepest approximation?  Does it always?
- In which situations do all the limiters give the same slope?  Why?

## Higher-order interpolation: WENO

If we want to get higher-order accuracy (in smooth regions), then we have to
give up the TVD property -- at least, in the sense defined above.  The most
common approach for higher order non-oscillatory piecewise interpolation is
known as weighted essentially non-oscillatory (WENO) interpolation.

WENO is a very effective technique for interpolating or reconstructing
functions that contain discontinuities without introducing oscillations.
We'll focus on 5th-order WENO interpolation, which is the most commonly used.
As for the limiters above, we work with point values of a function.  (In
finite volume methods, WENO is usually applied instead to cell averages; the
idea is the same, but the coefficients are different.)

We take 5 values $y_{i-2}, \dots, y_{i+2}$ at the points $x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2$
(so $x_i = 0$ and $\Delta x = 1$).  You can change them with the sliders
below, or choose one of the preset data sets.  The plots that follow use these
values, until the final plot of this section, which has its own controls.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof wenoPreset = Inputs.radio(["Example", "Step", "Random"], {value: "Example", label: "Data"})
viewof wenoReroll = Inputs.button("New random data")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Helpers shared by the two sets of WENO data controls.
function wenoPresetValues(preset) {
  if (preset === "Example") return [0.262, 0.298, 0.814, 0.092, 0.600];
  if (preset === "Step") return [1, 1, 1, 0, 0];
  if (preset === "Random") return d3.range(5).map(() => Math.round(1000 * Math.random()) / 1000);
  throw new Error("Unrecognized preset: " + preset);
}
function wenoSliders(start) {
  return Inputs.form(start.map((v, j) =>
    Inputs.range([-0.5, 2], {value: v, step: 0.001,
      label: tex`y_{i${j === 2 ? "" : (j < 2 ? "-" : "+") + Math.abs(j - 2)}}`})));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
wenoStart = { wenoReroll; return wenoPresetValues(wenoPreset); }
viewof wenoY = wenoSliders(wenoStart)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
weno = {
  const xs = [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2];

  // Solve A c = b by Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting.
  function solve(A, b) {
    const n = b.length, M = A.map((row, i) => [...row, b[i]]);
    for (let col = 0; col < n; col++) {
      let piv = col;
      for (let r = col + 1; r < n; r++) if (Math.abs(M[r][col]) > Math.abs(M[piv][col])) piv = r;
      [M[col], M[piv]] = [M[piv], M[col]];
      for (let r = col + 1; r < n; r++) {
        const f = M[r][col] / M[col][col];
        for (let c = col; c <= n; c++) M[r][c] -= f * M[col][c];
      }
    }
    const c = new Array(n);
    for (let r = n - 1; r >= 0; r--) {
      let s = M[r][n];
      for (let j = r + 1; j < n; j++) s -= M[r][j] * c[j];
      c[r] = s / M[r][r];
    }
    return c;
  }
  // Coefficients a_0, a_1, ... of the interpolating polynomial sum_j a_j x^j.
  const polyfit = (px, py) => solve(px.map(t => px.map((_, j) => t ** j)), py);
  const peval = (a, t) => a.reduceRight((s, aj) => s * t + aj, 0);

  // Optimal weights (left, center, right) at x = -1/2 and x = +1/2, as computed
  // by compute_opt_weights in the notebook.  They are checked below.
  const gamma = {"-1": [5/16, 5/8, 1/16], "1": [1/16, 5/8, 5/16]};
  const eps = 1e-6;

  function analyze(y) {
    const quartic = polyfit(xs, y);
    const p = [0, 1, 2].map(r => polyfit(xs.slice(r, r + 3), y.slice(r, r + 3)));
    // Jiang-Shu smoothness indicator for p(x) = a0 + a1 x + a2 x^2 on [-1/2, 1/2]
    // with dx = 1:  int (p')^2 + int (p'')^2 = a1^2 + a2^2/3 + 4 a2^2.
    const beta = p.map(a => a[1] ** 2 + (13 / 3) * a[2] ** 2);
    const out = {quartic, p, beta, w: {}, q: {}};
    for (const loc of ["-1", "1"]) {
      const xe = +loc / 2, g = gamma[loc];
      const opt = d3.sum(p, (a, j) => g[j] * peval(a, xe));
      if (Math.abs(opt - peval(quartic, xe)) > 1e-9 * (1 + Math.abs(opt)))
        throw new Error(`optimal weights do not reproduce the quartic at x = ${xe}`);
      const wt = g.map((gj, j) => gj / (eps + beta[j]) ** 2);
      const tot = d3.sum(wt);
      out.w[loc] = wt.map(v => v / tot);
      out.q[loc] = d3.sum(p, (a, j) => out.w[loc][j] * peval(a, xe));
    }
    return out;
  }

  const names = ["left", "center", "right"];
  const colors = ["#1f77b4", "#d62728", "#2ca02c"];

  // Plot the data, the given polynomials (on [-2, 2], thicker on [-1/2, 1/2]),
  // and optionally the WENO values.
  function plot(y, polys, {colorList, values = null, height = 300} = {}) {
    const fine = d3.range(-2, 2.0001, 0.02), cell = d3.range(-0.5, 0.5001, 0.02);
    return Plot.plot({
      width: 700, height, marginTop: 10,
      x: {domain: [-2.5, 2.5], label: null},
      y: {domain: [-0.5, 2.1], label: null, grid: true},
      marks: [
        ...polys.flatMap((a, j) => [
          Plot.line(fine, {x: d => d, y: d => peval(a, d), stroke: colorList[j], strokeWidth: 1.5, clip: true}),
          Plot.line(cell, {x: d => d, y: d => peval(a, d), stroke: colorList[j], strokeWidth: 6, strokeOpacity: 0.5, clip: true})
        ]),
        Plot.dot(xs.map((t, i) => ({x: t, y: y[i]})), {x: "x", y: "y", r: 4, fill: "currentColor"}),
        values ? Plot.dot(values, {x: "x", y: "y", r: 10, fill: "gray", fillOpacity: 0.5, stroke: "currentColor"}) : null
      ]
    });
  }

  return {xs, polyfit, peval, gamma, analyze, names, colors, plot};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

```

Ordinary polynomial interpolation yields an oscillatory polynomial that, for
the example data, also exceeds the bounds of the data:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
weno.plot(wenoY, [wenoResult.quartic], {colorList: ["currentColor"]})
```

For application to hyperbolic conservation laws, our main interest is in
getting values of the function at the half-integer points (interfaces).
Let's suppose we're trying to interpolate around $x=0$, at $x=\pm 1/2$.
Instead of using all 5 points, we could just use three points, which might
give us a less oscillatory interpolant, at least in that interval.  Using the
5 points we're given, there are three natural choices of interpolation
stencil: the leftmost three, the middle three, or the rightmost three.  Let's
see what each of these quadratic interpolants looks like.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`${[0, 1, 2].map(j => html`<div style="margin-bottom: .5rem">
  <strong style="color: ${weno.colors[j]}">${weno.names[j]} interpolant</strong>
  ${weno.plot(wenoY, [wenoResult.p[j]], {colorList: [weno.colors[j]], height: 200})}</div>`)}`
```

Here are all three quadratic interpolants together with the quartic
interpolant for comparison:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
weno.plot(wenoY, [...wenoResult.p, wenoResult.quartic], {colorList: [...weno.colors, "currentColor"]})
```

The quadratic interpolants look less oscillatory, but they're also less
accurate.  The WENO idea is to use the high-order interpolant (with all 5
points) if the data is smooth, but to use one of the lower-order interpolants
(or a combination of them) if the data is not smooth.  This is achieved by
computing point values of the interpolant as weighted averages of the point
values of the candidate polynomials.  Let $p_1 = p_\text{left}$, $p_2 = p_\text{center}$,
and $p_3 = p_\text{right}$.  Writing $\tilde{y}_{i-1/2}$ for the interpolated
value at $x_{i-1/2}$,

$$\tilde{y}_{i-1/2} = \sum_{j=1}^{3} w_{j,-1/2}\, p_j(x_{i-1/2}).$$

Of course, there is some particular set of weights that gives the value of the
quartic interpolant:

$$p_\text{quartic}(x_{i-1/2}) = \sum_{j=1}^{3} \gamma_{j,-1/2}\, p_j(x_{i-1/2}).$$

These *optimal weights* $\gamma$ do not depend on the data, but they do depend
on the point where we evaluate.  Requiring this equation to hold for any data
gives

$$
\gamma_{j,-1/2} = \left(\tfrac{5}{16}, \tfrac{5}{8}, \tfrac{1}{16}\right), \qquad
\gamma_{j,+1/2} = \left(\tfrac{1}{16}, \tfrac{5}{8}, \tfrac{5}{16}\right)
$$

for $j = 1, 2, 3$.

We will want to have $w_{j,\pm 1/2} \approx \gamma_{j,\pm 1/2}$ for smooth
data.

How does one determine if a polynomial is non-oscillatory?  There are several
ways proposed in the literature, but the original and most widely used is the
weighted Sobolev norm introduced by Jiang and Shu:

$$\beta = \sum_{l=1}^{k-1} \Delta x^{2l-1} \int_{x_{i-1/2}}^{x_{i+1/2}} \left(\frac{d^l}{dx^l}p(x)\right)^2 dx.$$

Here $k = 3$ is the number of points in each candidate stencil.  Put simply,
$\beta$ is a scaled sum of the squared $L^2$ norms of all the derivatives of
the polynomial over the interval where it will be used.  The scaling is
chosen to make the "smoothness indicator" $\beta$ independent of the choice
of $\Delta x$.

As each of the interpolants above is a linear function of the values $y_j$,
the smoothness indicators are quadratic functions of the $y_j$.  If we number
the stencils $r = 0, 1, 2$ from left to right, so that stencil $r$ uses
$y_{i-2+r}, y_{i-1+r}, y_{i+r}$, they can be written in the form

$$\beta_r = \sum_{m=0}^{2} \sum_{n=0}^{m} C_{r,m,n}\, y_{i-2+r+m}\, y_{i-2+r+n}.$$

The coefficients $C_{r,m,n}$ are different for each of the candidate
polynomials $p_\text{left},p_\text{center},p_\text{right}$.  Here we simply
compute $\beta$ directly from each polynomial.

Next we use these smoothness indicators to determine a weighting for the
candidate polynomials.  Observe that a large smoothness indicator means a
polynomial has large derivatives, so we will want to give it less weight
(perhaps they should be called non-smoothness indicators).

$$\tilde{w}_j = \frac{\gamma_j}{(\epsilon + \beta_j)^2}$$

Here $\epsilon$ is a small number used to avoid division by zero; we use
$\epsilon = 10^{-6}$.  We also normalize the weights so that they sum to
unity:

$$w_j = \frac{\tilde{w}_j}{\sum_j\tilde{w}_j}$$

<details>
<summary>Python code from the notebook</summary>

```python
def stencil_coefficients(xs,xe):
    """Coefficients c such that the polynomial interpolating (xs[j], f_j)
       has the value sum_j c[j]*f_j at the point xe."""
    n = len(xs)
    V = np.vander(xs,n,increasing=True)
    return np.linalg.solve(V.T, xe**np.arange(n))

def compute_opt_weights(x,k,xi):
    """
    Optimal (linear) weights gamma for the k candidate stencils (ordered left, center, right)
    at the points x_i + xi/2, where x_i is the middle point of x.  These are the weights
    for which the combination of the degree-(k-1) interpolants equals the degree-(2k-2)
    interpolant through all 2k-1 points.
    """
    gamma = {}
    for xi_val in xi:
        xe = x[k-1] + xi_val/2.
        c_opt = stencil_coefficients(x,xe)
        M = np.zeros((2*k-1,k))
        for r in range(k):
            M[r:r+k,r] = stencil_coefficients(x[r:r+k],xe)
        g = np.linalg.lstsq(M,c_opt,rcond=None)[0]
        assert np.allclose(M.dot(g),c_opt), 'no exact optimal weights at xi = %s' % xi_val
        gamma[xi_val] = g
    return gamma

def compute_smoothness_indicators(polys,dx=1.):
    "Jiang-Shu smoothness indicator of each polynomial on the interval [-dx/2, dx/2]."
    beta = np.zeros(len(polys))
    for r, poly in enumerate(polys):
        degree = poly.order
        for l in range(1,degree+1):
            antiderivative = np.polyint(np.polyder(poly,l)**2)
            beta[r] += dx**(2*l-1) * (antiderivative(dx/2.) - antiderivative(-dx/2.))
    return beta

def compute_weights(gamma, beta, epsilon=1.e-6):
    k = len(beta)
    w = np.empty(k)
    for j in range(k):
        w[j] = gamma[j]/(epsilon+beta[j])**2

    wsum = np.sum(w)
    return w/wsum
```

</details>

## Comparison of several limiters for advection

In practice, all of these limiters are used as components of numerical solvers
for hyperbolic PDEs.  The simplest hyperbolic PDE is the advection equation:

$$ q_t + a q_x = 0.$$

The solution $q$ simply translates at velocity $a$; if you're not familiar
with this, take a look at my
[HyperPython lesson on advection](https://nbviewer.org/github/ketch/HyperPython/blob/master/Lesson_01_Advection.ipynb)
and then the
[lesson on high-resolution methods](https://nbviewer.org/github/ketch/HyperPython/blob/master/Lesson_03_High-resolution_methods.ipynb).

The plots below show solutions of the advection equation with $a = 1$ on the
interval $[0, 1]$ with periodic boundary conditions, using 100 grid cells and
several of the methods we've discussed.  The TVD limiters are used in
Clawpack's second-order finite volume method; "Lax-Wendroff" is the same
method with no limiter, and "first-order" is the upwind method.  The WENO
solutions use the method of lines with WENO reconstruction of order 5, 7, or
9.  These solutions were computed with PyClaw, using the code in the notebook;
the solution advects across the full domain once in each unit of time.  The
grey curve is the initial condition, which is also the exact solution after
each full cycle.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
advection = FileAttachment("limiters_advection.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof advFrame = {
  const n = advection.cycles * advection.framesPerCycle;
  const form = html`<div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: .75rem; flex-wrap: wrap">
    <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" style="min-width: 4.5rem">Play</button>
    <input type="range" min="0" max="${n}" step="1" value="0" style="flex: 1; min-width: 10rem">
    <output style="min-width: 7rem"></output></div>`;
  const [button, range, output] = form.querySelectorAll("button, input, output");
  let timer = null;
  const show = v => {
    form.value = v;
    output.value = `t = ${(v / advection.framesPerCycle).toFixed(1)} cycles`;
  };
  const stop = () => { clearInterval(timer); timer = null; button.textContent = "Play"; };
  range.oninput = () => show(+range.value);  // the input event then bubbles to the form
  button.onclick = () => {
    if (timer) return stop();
    if (+range.value >= n) range.value = 0;
    button.textContent = "Pause";
    timer = setInterval(() => {
      range.value = +range.value + 1;
      show(+range.value);
      form.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
      if (+range.value >= n) stop();
    }, 120);
  };
  invalidation.then(() => clearInterval(timer));
  show(0);
  return form;
}
```

  const rows = (frame) => names.flatMap(name => {

  <tbody>${Object.entries(advection.schemes).map(([name, s]) =>

By stepping through the animation, you can see how each limiter modifies the
shape of the solution over time.  The Lax-Wendroff method is based on a
centered-difference approximation with no limiting; notice that it creates
oscillations and is also less accurate than the limiter-based methods.  For
the advection equation, oscillations and overshoots are not a serious problem,
but in the context of fluid dynamics or water wave simulations, they can be
catastrophic.
